title: Send scouts, then follow the footprints
allegory: Monte Carlo tree search is like sending scouts one at a time from base camp into a maze of caves: each picks forks by the best reports so far plus a guidebook tip that fades as the fork gets busy, asks a judge at the first new cave how things look, and chalks the verdict on every fork on the way home, so the fork with the most footprints becomes your move.
map: one scout's round trip from camp
one simulation from the root: select, expand, evaluate, back up
picking a fork: best reports so far, plus a guidebook tip that fades as the fork gets busy
the judge at the first new cave
the value head v(s) at the new leaf, or the true result z if the game is over
chalking every fork on the way home, plus for the chooser's good news and minus for bad
backup: N += 1 and W += v on each edge, with v's sign flipped at every ply
the fork at camp with the most footprints
the most-visited root move: the improved policy you play

cap.1: Your move in Connect 4. Seven columns, seven replies to each, seven more after that. You know the rules, so you can imagine any future, just not all of them.
cap.2: DQN and PPO learn the world from experience. MCTS assumes you already have a simulator (for a board game, the rules) and spends it on thinking before each move.
cap.3: MCTS is model-based planning: with a simulator in hand, grow a search tree rooted at the current state. Exhaustive lookahead is hopeless, so the real question is where to spend a fixed simulation budget.

cap.1: Send scouts one at a time. Each walks the mapped tunnels, steps into one new cave, asks the judge how it looks, then walks home chalking every fork.
cap.2: One simulation: select (walk down the tree), expand (add one node), evaluate (get a value), back up (update every edge on the path). Repeat, then play the root move with the most visits.
cap.3: Each edge stores visit count N(s,a), value sum W(s,a) and mean Q = W / max(1, N). After sims rounds, the root visit counts are the improved policy: play the argmax, or sample from N^(1/τ) in self-play.

parts.note: how it has done so far
fades as this fork gets busy

cap.1: At each fork the scout adds two things: how well that tunnel has done so far, and the guidebook's tip for it. The tip fades as more scouts try that tunnel.
cap.2: PUCT: Q is the measured average value. The second term is big for moves the policy network likes that haven't been tried much, and shrinks as N grows: follow the network early, trust measurements later.
cap.3: PUCT(s,a) = Q + c_puct·p_θ(a|s)·√(1 + ΣN) / (1 + N(s,a)). The +1 under the root matters on a node's first visit: without it every bonus is 0 and argmax takes the first legal column, ignoring the prior.

cap.1: The judge says the new cave favours you. Walking home, the scout marks + at forks you chose and − at forks your rival chose. Your good news is their bad news.
cap.2: Backup walks the path in reverse: each edge gets N += 1 and W += v, with v's sign flipped at each ply, because each edge is scored for the player who chose it. Q = W / N is a running average.
cap.3: Negamax backup: alternate the sign of v by ply so Q(s,a) is always from the perspective of the player to move at s. At a terminal leaf, back up the true result z ∈ {−1, 0, +1} instead of v(s).

forks: PUCT with the policy prior

chapters.verdict: Starting from random play, it beat the published AlphaGo 100-0.

cap.1: Old scouts judged a new cave by wandering randomly to the game's end. AlphaGo Zero asked a trained judge and let hunches guide the forks. It won 100-0.
cap.2: Classic MCTS estimates a leaf with a random playout. AlphaGo Zero (Silver et al., Nature 2017) reads v(s) off the value head and selects with PUCT. From random play, with no human games, it won 100-0 against the published AlphaGo.
cap.3: Two departures from vanilla MCTS: v(s) replaces the rollout (the true z at terminal leaves), and the policy prior enters selection. Same four-phase skeleton, different leaf estimate and tree policy.

cap.1: The classic bug: from the second trip on, every scout takes the same tunnel. The rest barely get a look, so a wrong first guess never gets corrected.
cap.2: PUCT's two terms are on different scales. If c_puct is small next to the value range [−1, 1], or the prior is already sharp, the first move to score positive outbids every sibling's bonus for good.
cap.3: Fix: scale c_puct to the value head's range (ARENA: 1.0 with v ∈ [−1, 1]); add Dirichlet noise at the root only, P = (1 − ε)P + εη with ε = 0.25; log the root visit histogram. Healthy puts mass on 2 or 3 columns.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: The search teaches the network: AlphaZero
PUCT is the bandit's UCB on every fork

cap.1: The footprints beat the guidebook, so AlphaZero trains its network to copy them. Knowing how an AI plans is part of understanding and steering it.
cap.2: Root visit counts are an improved policy. AlphaZero trains a network to imitate the search, then searches with the better network. A planning system's choice comes from its judge, its hunches and its budget together.
cap.3: PUCT is UCB's exploit-plus-uncertainty split on tree edges, weighted by a learned prior. To understand or steer a planning agent, inspect every lever: value head, policy prior, c_puct and the simulation budget.

coda.title: Seven moves, one budget: where do the scouts go? (toy, one level deep)

params.label: how sure the guidebook is (prior sharpness)

readouts.label: share of scouts on e, the truly best move

caption.1: Each move has a fixed verdict; the guidebook likes d, but e is truly best. Drag the three sliders and watch where the footprints pile up.
caption.2: At c_puct = 1 and 16 sims, visits sit on c, d and e, with e ahead. Drop c_puct to 0.1: d takes every scout, even at 64. Sharpen the guidebook to 3: e gets no visits until about 40 sims.
caption.3: Score = Q + c·p·√(1 + ΣN) / (1 + N), Q = the move's verdict once tried, else 0; ties go to the first move. Bars are root visit shares. Lock-in comes from a small c against the value range or a sharp p.

where_else: AlphaZero: train a network to imitate the search's visit counts, then search again with the better network
Multi-armed bandits [2.1]: PUCT is UCB's exploit-plus-uncertainty split, moved onto the edges of a tree
Beam search in text generation: another way to grow only the promising branches of a tree of continuations

hamming.what: A planning method that grows a search tree from the current position, sends each simulation down the most promising path, and plays the move the search visited most.
hamming.when: When you have the rules or a simulator and some thinking time before each move, as in board games like Go and Connect 4.
hamming.why: You can't check every future, so splitting a fixed budget between what has worked and what looks promising lets a small search play strongly.

object.title: The footprint terrace
object.subtitle: Rows are moments in a search, from 2 scouts to 64; columns are seven moves; height is each move's share of the footprints.

cap.1: Each row is a moment in the search, from 2 scouts to 64. Each column is a move, a to g. Height is the share of scouts that took that fork so far.
cap.2: Bar height = root visit share N(a) / sims after 2, 4, ... 64 simulations of a toy one-level search where each move has a fixed verdict.
cap.3: A toy root-only PUCT search (a bandit): fixed leaf value per move, prior p, c_puct knob. Heights are normalised root visit counts, the improved policy.

cap.1: Early scouts follow the guidebook to d. As verdicts come in, e, which the guidebook undersold, takes over: half the scouts by 16, most of them by 64.
cap.2: With c_puct = 1, the prior's favourite d gets the first visits; e's higher Q wins once it is tried. At 16 sims visits sit on c, d and e: a healthy spread.
cap.3: PUCT follows the prior while every Q is 0, then measured Q takes over as the 1/(1 + N) bonus decays: 8 of 16 visits, then 47 of 64, land on e.

cap.1: Turn the exploration dial nearly off. d's first positive verdict outbids every other tip: one spike, from 2 scouts all the way to 64.
cap.2: c_puct too small next to the value range: d's Q = +0.2 beats every sibling's shrunken bonus, so nothing else is tried. More sims change nothing.
cap.3: At c = 0.1 the best sibling bonus, 0.1·0.2·√(1 + ΣN), stays under Q_d = 0.2 for all 64 sims: the self-confirming lock-in, since untried moves never earn a Q.

cap.1: Back to the normal dial, but make the guidebook overconfident. The scouts crowd d, e gets its first visit only after about 40, and at 64 d still leads.
cap.2: A sharp prior shrinks every sibling's bonus. Cube the prior and renormalise: e is unvisited through 32 sims. The search only explores what the network already likes.
cap.3: The run-level version of this collapse is why self-play adds Dirichlet noise at the root: the search explores what the network likes, and the network learns only what the search explores.

cap.1: Now turn the dial way up. Scouts keep chasing tips and spread out, so at 16 scouts d still edges e. Too much exploring spends the budget thinly.
cap.2: Large c_puct: the prior term dominates for longer and visits track p. At 16 sims d leads; e only pulls ahead with more sims.
cap.3: As c_puct grows the visit shares drift toward the prior; as it shrinks, toward greedy on the first Q found. ARENA tuned c_puct down from 1.5 to 1.0 with a full-run sweep.

cap.1: Back to the tuned dial. That share of footprints is the plan: AlphaZero trains its network to copy it, then sends better-guided scouts.
cap.2: Root visit counts, not the raw prior, are what you play (argmax) or sample in self-play (N^(1/τ)); AlphaZero trains the network to imitate them.
cap.3: Visit counts improve on p_θ; training toward them and searching again is the AlphaZero loop, with the search acting as teacher.

predict.q: After 16 scouts, which move do you play?

options.t: The one the most scouts took
The one the guidebook liked best
The one with the single best verdict ever seen

predict.why: Visit counts blend the hunch with measured results, so they are the improved policy. In ARENA you play the most-visited column.

predict.q: c_puct is tiny and the first move tried scores positive. What do more scouts do?

options.t: Nothing: that move keeps taking every scout
They slowly spread to the other moves

predict.why: Its Q beats every sibling's small bonus, so nothing else is tried and nothing else earns a Q. The spike confirms itself.

predict.q: Why does the chalk mark flip sign at every fork on the way home?

options.t: Players alternate, and each fork is scored for whoever chooses there
To stop the numbers growing too big

predict.why: Negamax: a position that is good for your rival is bad for you.

object.where: Anywhere a fixed budget is split between what has worked and what looks promising: bandits, beam search, planning agents.
